results.title: Causal Effects via Propensity Scores | Towards Data Science
results.content:
Title: Causal Effects via Propensity Scores | Towards Data Science
# Causal Effects via Propensity Scores. Namely, *how can we compute causal effects from observational data?* Here, I will discuss a set of techniques that do exactly this using something called a propensity score. Propensity scores estimate the probability of treatment. A **propensity score** estimates the **probability a subject** **receives a particular treatment based on other characteristics** (i.e. covariates). Armed with this dataset, we can obtain a propensity score via a logistic regression model in a straightforward way. Once we have a logistic regression model, we can obtain a probability of treatment (i.e. propensity score) for each subject in the dataset. Now that we know what a propensity score is and how to compute it, we turn to **how to use a propensity score to estimate causal effects**. In other words, pick a treated subject and match them to an untreated subject with the closest propensity score one by one. **Stratification** of the propensity score **splits subjects into groups with similar propensity scores** in which causal effects can be computed. Once we have stratified the subject based on the PS, we can compute treatment effects by **directly comparing treated and untreated populations within each group** as before. In matching and stratification, we use the propensity score to derive *subject groups* which can be used to compute treatment effects. With IPTW, however, **we use the propensity scores to derive *weights for each subject* which are then used to compute treatment effects directly**. Before moving on to the example code, it is worth mentioning that propensity score-based methods are not our only option when trying to compute causal effects from observational data. ## **Example: Estimating Treatment Effect of Grad School on Income (with propensity scores)**. In this example, we will estimate the causal effect of a graduate degree on income using the 3 propensity score methods discussed earlier. Then, we can finally use each propensity score method to estimate the causal effect of hasGraduateDegree on greaterThan50k. [2] The central role of the propensity score in observational studies for causal effects by Paul R.

results.title: Propensity-Score Matching Is the Bedrock of Causal Statistics
results.content:
Title: Propensity-Score Matching Is the Bedrock of Causal Statistics
# Propensity-Score Matching Is the Bedrock of Causal Statistics. Propensity-Score Matching (PSM) is a well-established approach to explaining causality in data. We will cover its theory, how to implement it in Python, and some recent advancements in causal statistics that complement PSM.*. Or would better-performing people want to undergo a training program, and hence we only see an effect due to selection bias? Propensity-Score Matching (PSM) is one of the older ones, having emerged around 40 years ago. A key advantage of PSM is that it allows researchers to work with real-world data. Data professionals who work with real-world data but do not have their grips on causal statistics are really missing out on a lot of potential insights. ## Propensity-Score Matching, or How to Estimate Treatment Effects. Propensity-Score Matching is not as elemental and easy-to-grasp as a linear regression. As such, it is important to first understand what propensity scores are, and how to match them. ### Propensity Scores. A propensity score is quite simply the probability of receiving some treatment T given a set of observed covariates X (i.e. variables that influence this probability). where e is the propensity score for receiving treatment (T=1 means treatment received, T=0 no treatment). If one conditions the propensity score, then one can make the treatment and the non-treatment group comparable. One can estimate such scores with simple logistic regression models, or, when a lot of data is available, machine learning algorithms like decision trees or boosted vector machines. * Nearest Neighbor Matching: Each treated unit is matched with the untreated unit with the closest propensity score. * Caliper Matching: Only matches an untreated unit with a treated unit if the latter is in the range (also called caliper) of this unit’s propensity score. * Stratification or subclassification: The space of possible propensity scores is divided into bins and the treatment effects within each bin (also called stratum) are estimated separately. The goal of all these techniques is to tease out the treatment effect by keeping the influence X as similar as possible between treatment and control units. PSM is powerful because it avoids selection bias; all kinds of covariates X can be taken into account after all.

results.title: Addressing confounding errors when using non-experimental, observational data to make causal claims | Synthese | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Addressing confounding errors when using non-experimental, observational data to make causal claims | Synthese | Springer Nature Link
Although we are not sanguine about the difficulty in using observational data to make warranted causal claims, we are not as pessimistic as those who believe that the only warranted causal claims are claims based on data from (idealized) RCTs. We argue that careful, thoughtful study design, informed by expert knowledge, that incorporates propensity score matching methods in conjunction with instrumental variable analyses, provides the possibility of warranted causal claims using observational data. Propensity score matching is a causal inference technique that attempts to balance treatment groups on confounding factors, so researchers can gauge the treatment’s causal impact on the outcome.
